While easy and non-invasive, veterinarians and scientific organizations emphasize that hair testing is not scientifically validated for diagnosing true allergies or intolerances.Sample collection: You pluck 20 to 25 strands of hair (including the root) from your pet and mail them in a provided bag.Technology: The company uses bioresonance testing to scan hair samples against hundreds of food and environmental items.Results delivery: Digital color-coded results arrive via email within 5 to 7 days, ranking items from severe intolerance (red) to no response (gray).Pros and ConsProsConvenient: Done at home without a stressful vet visit or blood draw.Broad scope: Screens over 270 food items and numerous environmental triggers.Helpful starting point: Some owners use the results as a loose guide to experiment with rotation or elimination diets.ConsLack of scientific backing: Major veterinary and allergy groups state hair analysis cannot measure current bodily sensitivities or true food allergies.False positives/negatives: Many pet owners report that results label an overwhelming number of everyday items as "intolerant," making strict avoidance nearly impossible.Not diagnostic: 5Strands explicitly states their kits are for guidance only and not a substitute for formal veterinary diagnosis.What Veterinarians Recommend InsteadElimination diet trials: Feeding a strict prescription or novel-protein diet for 8 to 12 weeks is the gold standard for diagnosing food sensitivities.Veterinary allergy testing: Blood (serum) or skin (intradermal) testing performed by a veterinary dermatologist is recommended for environmental allergies.If you're considering this test, tell me:What symptoms is your pet having (itching, ear infections, vomiting)?Have you tried a dietary elimination trial yet?If you're considering this test, tell me: Learn moreCopied to clipboardFailed to copy to clipboard.
